prompt.context: A chemical company's profits have been falling recently.
prompt.question: How would you advise the company to improve profits?

clarifying_info.a: No. Our costs have been constant.

clarifying_info.q: Does our company sell just one product or do we sell multiple products?
clarifying_info.a: Multiple products. We sell generics and specialty drugs.

clarifying_info.q: Have we noticed a decline in revenues on both lines of products, or just one?
clarifying_info.a: Our competitors have cut prices on similar generics. We've had to cut prices to match or risk losing customers.

clarifying_info.q: Are we still profitable on the generics?
clarifying_info.a: No. Our prices are below our costs on the generics. We don't have (and cannot gain) the economies of scale to match our competitors. As a result, our costs are prohibitively high.

clarifying_info.q: Are we profitable on the specialty drugs?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Specialty drugs are highly profitable. Economies of scale are less important in driving down the costs of specialty drugs.

framework: Start with a cost-revenue / profitability framework
Diagnose whether the profit decline stems from rising costs or falling revenues
If revenues, determine which product lines are affected and why
Assess competitive dynamics and cost structure for each product line
Evaluate strategic options: exit unprofitable segments, double down on profitable ones

questions.prompt: Is the profit decline driven by costs or revenues?
questions.guidance: Costs are constant, so the issue is entirely on the revenue side. Candidate should quickly confirm this and pivot to revenue analysis.

questions.prompt: Which product line is causing the revenue decline?
questions.guidance: The company sells two product lines: generics and specialty drugs. Generics prices have been cut by competitors, forcing the client to match prices. Specialty drugs remain profitable. Candidate should identify that the problem is isolated to generics.

questions.prompt: What is the profitability position of each product line?
questions.guidance: Generics: prices now below cost — the company cannot achieve sufficient economies of scale to compete. Specialty drugs: highly profitable, and economies of scale are not a major cost driver in this segment. The key insight is that generics are structurally loss-making while specialty drugs are structurally profitable.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions should the client take to improve profits?

categories.name: Exit generics
ideas: Reorient or close unprofitable generic-drug factories
Avoid further price wars where scale economics are unfavorable

categories.name: Double down on specialty drugs
ideas: Concentrate capital and management attention on specialty markets
Reorient sales force toward specialty drugs
Enhance distribution efforts for specialty drugs
Modify sales incentives to encourage specialty drug sales

categories.name: Cost reduction (secondary)
ideas: Evaluate whether any fixed costs from generics can be repurposed for specialty production
Assess severance and plant closure costs vs. ongoing losses from generics

recommendation: End production of generic drugs — prices are below cost and the company cannot close the economies-of-scale gap with competitors
Reorient or close the unprofitable generic-drug factories
Concentrate all efforts on profitable specialty drug markets, where economies of scale are not a decisive factor
risks: Plant closure and workforce restructuring costs could be significant in the short term
Customers who buy both generics and specialty drugs from the client may shift their specialty business elsewhere if the generic relationship ends
Regulatory or contractual obligations may constrain how quickly the client can exit generics
next_steps: Quantify the ongoing losses from generics vs. the one-time exit costs to confirm exit is value-positive
Map existing customer relationships to assess specialty drug revenue at risk from exiting generics
Develop a sales force reorientation and incentive restructuring plan for the specialty segment
